planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Catucaí is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Bred in Brazil beginning in the 1980s from a cross of Catuaí and Icatu, Catucaí combines the compact, manageable stature and heavy productivity of Catuaí with genetic material from the taller, more disease-tolerant Icatu (itself an old Typica x Bourbon x robusta-derived line), producing a vigorous, high-yielding, fairly compact Arabica selection favored on Brazilian smallholdings for its productivity and adaptability across a range of elevations. Several numbered Catucaí sub-selections exist, differing slightly in vigor, bean size, and cup profile, but all share the parent cross's combination of good yield and manageable size. Grow it in the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions as other Arabica coffees, feed regularly to sustain heavy bearing on a compact frame, and expect the first cherries after three to four years.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5-6.5) soil in part shade; Coffea eugenioides is a cool-highland understory species that prefers milder temperatures and more shade than lowland C. canephora, performing best where summer heat is moderated.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade; Coffea eugenioides is a small understory tree native to the montane forests of the African Great Lakes region (Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, eastern DR Congo), where it grows at higher, cooler elevations than either of the two dominant commercial species. It holds a special place in coffee genetics as one of the two wild parent species — alongside C. canephora (robusta) — whose ancient natural hybridization produced C. arabica; as such it carries genetic interest for breeders working on climate resilience and novel flavor profiles. Its beans are notably small and its leaves narrow and glossy, and the species is distinguished by unusually low caffeine content (roughly a quarter that of typical arabica), making it a subject of recent specialty-coffee interest in naturally low-caffeine coffee breeding. Rarely offered outside botanical collections and specialty coffee research nurseries, it is grown by collectors and rare-fruit enthusiasts in zone 10-12 tropical gardens under the same filtered-shade, humid conditions as other coffee species, with tolerance for slightly cooler nights than lowland types.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online

common_name: Tricolor Shell Ginger (Pink-Cream-and-Green Variegated Tropical Ginger)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to fairly deep shade; Tricolor Shell Ginger needs more shade protection than the green species or the cream-and-green Variegata, since its pink streaking is especially prone to scorch in direct Gulf South sun.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to fairly deep shade; Tricolor Shell Ginger is a striking sport of the familiar green-and-cream Variegated Shell Ginger, adding streaks and splashes of soft pink to the existing cream-and-green variegation for a softer, more painterly three-color effect on the same broad, strap-shaped leaves. The pink pigmentation is most pronounced on new growth in cooler weather and on plants grown in bright, dappled shade rather than deep shade or full sun, fading somewhat as leaves mature and as summer heat intensifies. Slower-growing and slightly less vigorous than the plain green species or the cream-variegated form, it is best used as a shaded specimen or accent rather than a fast-filling mass planting. In zone 9, established clumps are top-killed by hard freezes but return reliably from the rhizome each spring; mulch heavily over winter in zone 8-9a gardens, and divide congested clumps in spring to maintain vigor and color intensity.
